records.place: Vila Nogueira de Azeitão, Setúbal, Península de Setúbal

wine.name: Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal
wine.grapes: Moscatel de Setúbal, the local name for Muscat of Alexandria, alone, by the house's sheets.
wine.sites: The house's Moscatel vineyards of the peninsula, on the clay and limestone by the Serra da Arrábida and on the sandy plain, the two soils its sheets name for the grape.
wine.making: The must begins to ferment on its skins, and grape spirit is added to stop it while much of the sugar remains. The wine then stays on its skins for months, three to five by vintage on the house's sheets, before it is drawn off. It ages in used wooden casks and vats, and is bottled with the year of its harvest.
wine.glass: Amber gold; candied orange peel and Moscatel raisins over honey, sweet and grapey, with the freshness the house credits to the Arrábida and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Bottled ready to drink, it does not develop further in bottle, by the house's sheet, so drink it young; the aged blends of the range carry their years on the label.
wine.serve: About 10 degrees Celsius as an aperitif and up to 16 degrees Celsius after dinner, by the house's sheet; no decanting; a small white wine glass.

label.means: The estate where the founder first planted Moscatel, and a nod to the wine's amber colour, by the house's account.
A traditional name allowed only when Moscatel gives at least 85 per cent of the must.
Alambre carries the year of its harvest; the 20 Anos and the other aged blends carry an age instead.

records.table: José Maria da Fonseca's Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal is Muscat of Alexandria fortified while it ferments, then left on its skins for months and aged in old wood: candied orange peel and raisins, sweet yet fresh. Pour it cool as an aperitif, or a little warmer with dessert.
records.story: The house carries the name of its founder, a mathematician from the Dão, born in 1804 and trained at Coimbra, who settled at Vila Nogueira de Azeitão and there, in 1834 by the house's account, set up the company. By its own timeline he created its Moscatel de Setúbal brand in 1849, and he bought land across the peninsula, among it the Cova da Periquita, whose red was certainly being made by 1850. The house tells how, in the nineteenth century, merchant ships carried its Moscatel in cask to Brazil, Africa and India, and how the casks that came back unsold had improved on the voyage: the Torna Viagem, the wine of the return. In 1907 the Setúbal region was delimited for its Moscatel, and in 1944 the house created Lancers, a lightly sparkling rosé. In 2000 it revived the old voyage aboard the Sagres, the navy's training ship, comparing the travelled casks with casks kept at Azeitão, and it repeated the voyage in the years that followed. Among its special wines it keeps a Moscatel de Setúbal Superior of 1911 and a Moscatel Roxo of 1918. Alambre, named for the estate where the founder first planted Moscatel, is the house's plain statement of the style: months on the skins after fortification, then old wood.

others.name: Alambre 20 Anos
others.note: The house's twenty year old Moscatel de Setúbal, a blend of harvests left five months on the skins and aged in used wood.

others.name: Periquita
others.note: The red from the Cova da Periquita, made by 1850, whose name became a popular synonym for the Castelão grape.

others.name: Lancers
others.note: The lightly sparkling rosé the house created in 1944.

traps: José Maria da Fonseca of Azeitão is not Fonseca, the Port house of Vila Nova de Gaia: two families, two different wines.
Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal is fortified, its fermentation stopped with grape spirit, not a late harvest wine.
Periquita is the house's brand; the grape in the bottle is Castelão.

cards.front: José Maria da Fonseca: what is the Torna Viagem?
cards.back: Moscatel sent in cask to the tropics and back, an old custom the house revived in 2000 aboard the training ship Sagres.

cards.front: Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal: what happens to the wine after the spirit is added?
cards.back: It stays on its skins for months, three to five by vintage, and then ages in used wood.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives José Maria da Fonseca's Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal its depth of orange peel. Which step in its making explains it?
opts: Months on its skins after the spirit is added
A late harvest of shrivelled grapes
Fermentation to dryness, then sweetening
Ageing under a veil of flor yeast
questions.exp: The house stops the fermentation with grape spirit and leaves the wine on its skins for months, drawing aroma from them; it is not a late harvest wine, whose sweetness comes from shrivelled grapes.

questions.q: In 2000 José Maria da Fonseca sent casks of Moscatel to sea aboard the Sagres to revive an old custom of the house. What was it?
opts: The Torna Viagem, the wine of the return voyage
The estufa, a heated store that warms the casks
The solera, a tier of casks topped up each year
The canteiro, casks ageing high under a lodge roof
questions.exp: Merchant ships once carried the house's Moscatel to Brazil, Africa and India and brought casks back improved; the house revived that Torna Viagem in 2000. The estufa and canteiro belong to Madeira.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's share of 50, five on the house's own domain, with four more shared by the group (the Setúbal rules, the decree of 1992, the IVV's page and the identity of Moscatel Roxo); 46 of the 50 used in all; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the vintage dated Alambre Moscatel de Setúbal is taught, as the house's widely seen Moscatel, and the 20 Anos goes in others; the house's sheets give three months on the skins for the 2012 and 2019 and five for the 2008, hence three to five by vintage.

The founder's birth in 1804 is on the house's timeline and a second account, but his death is 1884 on the house's timeline and 1887 in another account, so the story describes him rather than naming him with dates; the house keeps his name.

1834 is the house's own year; one Portuguese paper says nobody knows the exact day and that 1834 is his entry in Lisbon's commercial association, so the story says by the house's account; 1849 and 1850 are the house's timeline and press dossier.

The Torna Viagem's nineteenth century story and the voyage of 2000 aboard the Sagres are the house's own pages; the later voyages (2007, 2010, 2015 to 2018, 2020) are counted differently on its pages, so the story says only that it repeated the voyage.
Lancers of 1944 is the house's timeline and Wikipedia; the Heublein link to Lancers was not found and is left out, as are the names of the descendants who created it.
Serving temperatures are the house's 2012 sheet; the Codex's service reference names no figure for a fortified Muscat.
No living person is named; the 1907 delimitation is the IVV's own page and the house's 2008 sheet.

wine.name: Quinta da Bacalhôa
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about nine tenths, with Merlot for the rest, by the company's recent sheets.
wine.sites: The vineyard planted in 1974 beside the Bacalhôa palace at Azeitão, on well drained sandy loam under a mild climate tempered by the Atlantic, by the company's sheets.
wine.making: The base wines ferment at controlled temperatures and rest about a week on their skins after fermentation. The final blend then ages in new French oak barrels, about a year in the vintages of the late 2010s and two years in recent ones, and at least six months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and blackberry with cedar, cigar box and a touch of tobacco and clove from the barrel; medium to full in body, with rounded tannin and a fresh, slightly savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release after its time in barrel and bottle, it also keeps for some years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the company advises; an hour in a decanter suits a young bottle; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate around the Renaissance palace at Azeitão, where the vineyard was planted in 1974.
The regional wine of the whole peninsula, with a wider list of grapes than its two DOCs.
Red; the estate also makes a white under the same name.

records.table: Quinta da Bacalhôa is the Cabernet of Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal: Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Merlot from a vineyard planted in 1974 beside a Renaissance palace at Azeitão, aged in new French oak. Expect blackcurrant and cedar, and pour it with red meat or game.
records.story: The palace that gives the company its name stands at Vila Fresca de Azeitão: a Renaissance house built after 1528 for the eldest son of the conqueror of Goa, its loggia lined with tile panels, one of them dated 1565. The name came only in the seventeenth century, from Bacalhau, the nickname of an heiress's husband, as the story goes. The company began apart from it, in 1922, as João Pires & Filhos, a family firm making wine in bulk. In the 1930s an American woman bought the palace and restored it, and in 1974, at the request of the palace's owners, an engineer planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot beside it, and the company made its wine. Its first vintage, 1979, was by the company's account the first Portuguese Cabernet Sauvignon, a red of Bordeaux grapes on a peninsula of Castelão and Moscatel. The firm traded as J.P. Vinhos; from 1998 it had new owners, it later took the palace's name as Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal, and around the turn of the millennium the palace and its quinta were bought as well, with a second red named for the palace. In 2007 the company added Caves Aliança in the Bairrada. Quinta da Bacalhôa remains its founding statement: Cabernet on the peninsula, aged in new French oak.

others.name: Palácio da Bacalhôa
others.note: A red of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Petit Verdot named for the palace, aged in new French oak.

others.name: Quinta da Bacalhôa Branco
others.note: The estate's white, made under the same name.

others.name: Moscatel de Setúbal Superior
others.note: The company's aged Moscatels of the peninsula, among them a Superior of ten years and one of thirty.

traps: Quinta da Bacalhôa is a Vinho Regional of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, not a DOC Palmela, whose reds are built on Castelão.
Quinta da Bacalhôa and Palácio da Bacalhôa are two different reds: the palace's wine adds Petit Verdot and came only after the turn of the millennium.

cards.front: Quinta da Bacalhôa: when was its vineyard planted, and when was its first vintage?
cards.back: Planted in 1974 beside the palace at Azeitão; the first vintage was 1979.

cards.front: Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal: under which two names did the company trade before?
cards.back: João Pires & Filhos, founded in 1922, and then J.P. Vinhos, before it took the palace's name.

questions.q: A guest is surprised to find a Bordeaux grape behind Quinta da Bacalhôa. What is the red mostly made from?
opts: Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Merlot
Castelão with a little Syrah
Touriga Nacional with Aragonez
Trincadeira with Alicante Bouschet
questions.exp: The company's sheets give about nine tenths Cabernet Sauvignon and the rest Merlot, from the vineyard planted in 1974; Castelão is the grape of DOC Palmela, not of this estate's red.

questions.q: A vineyard was planted beside the Bacalhôa palace at Azeitão in 1974. In which year was the first vintage of Quinta da Bacalhôa?
questions.exp: The company's sheets date the planting to 1974 and the first vintage to 1979; the palace and its quinta were bought by the company's owners only around the turn of the millennium.

report: Searches for this record: 10 of the group's share of 50, four on the company's own domain; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the vineyard was planted in 1974 and the first vintage was 1979, by the company's timeline and its sheets for the 2017 to 2023 vintages; its claim of the first Portuguese Cabernet Sauvignon is told as its own.

The rename to Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal is 1998 on the company's English timeline and 2005 on its Portuguese one and a second account, so the story gives no year; 1998 is the company's own year for its new owners, who are living and never named.

The American buyer of the palace is Orlena Scoville in one account and Mrs Herbert Scoville in another, and the year 1936 or 1937, so the story says an American woman in the 1930s; the owner at whose request the vines were planted and the engineer who planted them are not named for want of their dates.

The purchase of 1528 by the son of Afonso de Albuquerque and the building after it are in several accounts (Infopédia, an Azeitão guide, Wikipedia), though one old history gives a younger Afonso as the buyer, so the son is described, and neither man is named for want of firm dates; the nickname Bacalhau of the seventeenth century is Infopédia's and is hedged as the story goes.

Barrel time is 13 months for the 2017, 14 for the 2019, 18 for the 2020 and 24 for the 2021 and 2022 on the company's sheets, hence about a year to two years; the soil is sandy loam on the Portuguese sheets and limestone on one English sheet, and the record follows the Portuguese.
The glass rests on merchants' and reviewers' notes for the 2011, 2015, 2017 and 2022 and the company's own sheet; the decanting is one reviewer's advice.
The region record's Quinta da Bacalhôa Cabernet of the 1970s is borne out: planted in 1974, first vintage 1979.

records.place: Fernando Pó, Palmela, Península de Setúbal

wine.name: Dona Ermelinda Reserva Tinto
wine.grapes: Castelão from old vines, with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon; the blend shifts by vintage, Syrah taking a share in some.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards at Fernando Pó on the sandy plain of Palmela, the Castelão from vines of fifty years and more and the other grapes from younger plantings, by its merchants' sheets.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel with about twenty days on the skins, then aged about a year in French oak barrels and some eight months in bottle before release, by its merchants' sheets.
wine.glass: Dark berries in compote with smoke and a warm, spiced edge, and a touch of jam from its long maturation; dense and full in body, with soft, rounded tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Rounded and ready to drink on release, after its months in barrel and bottle, it keeps for a few years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young bottle needs no decanting; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The range named for the woman of the family's third generation who led the house.
The appellation of the sandy plain, whose reds are built on Castelão.
The house at Fernando Pó, named for the same woman.

records.table: Dona Ermelinda Reserva is the Palmela red of Casa Ermelinda Freitas, a family house at Fernando Pó led by women for four generations: old vine Castelão from the sand with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet, about a year in French oak. Dense and smoky, it suits roast meats.
records.story: Casa Ermelinda Freitas dates from 1920 at Fernando Pó, on the sandy plain of Palmela, and its line has run through the women of the family. The men died young, as the family tells it, and the farm passed from mother to daughter, from the founder to her daughter and then to the granddaughter for whom the house is named. For almost eighty years it sold its wine in bulk. That third woman, widowed when her husband died, kept the vineyards going with her daughter's help, and in the 1990s, after her father's death, the daughter came home from a career in social services and took the house in hand. She chose bottles over bulk, and the house began to sell its wine under its own labels, the range named for her mother, Dona Ermelinda, among them. Castelão has stayed at the heart of the vineyard, the grape of the Palmela DOC on sand, and the Dona Ermelinda Reserva blends that old vine Castelão with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon and gives it about a year in French oak. In 2020 the house marked a hundred years of wine. For a sommelier the Reserva is the Palmela of a family house: Castelão from the sand, made by the fourth generation of a house of women.

others.name: Dona Ermelinda Grande Reserva
others.note: A red of Syrah, Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Aragonez, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon, each aged apart for eighteen months in French oak.

others.name: Dona Ermelinda Reserva Branco
others.note: The white of the same range.

traps: Dona Ermelinda is the range and Casa Ermelinda Freitas the house: both honour the same woman of the family's third generation.
A DOC Palmela red is built on Castelão; the Dona Ermelinda Reserva keeps old vine Castelão at its heart and adds Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.front: Casa Ermelinda Freitas: which grape lies at the heart of the Dona Ermelinda Reserva?
cards.back: Castelão from old vines on the Palmela sand, with Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.front: How has Casa Ermelinda Freitas passed from one generation to the next since 1920?
cards.back: Through the women of the family, mother to daughter, for four generations.

questions.q: A guest asks which grape gives Casa Ermelinda Freitas's Dona Ermelinda Reserva its Palmela character. Which is it?

Baga
Alvarinho

questions.exp: Palmela's reds are built on Castelão, and the house uses it from old vines on the sand; Baga is the red grape of the Bairrada, not of the peninsula.

questions.q: For almost eighty years after 1920 Casa Ermelinda Freitas sold its wine in one way, before it turned to bottles in the 1990s. How did it sell it?
opts: In bulk
To the co-operative
As must for distilling
To the Port shippers
questions.exp: The house sold its wine in bulk for almost eighty years; in the 1990s the fourth generation turned it to bottled wine under its own labels, not to the co-operative.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's share of 50, three on the house's own domain, one of them wasted on a query with no result; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1920 is the house's own year and Portugal Global's; the red taught is the Dona Ermelinda Reserva, DOC Palmela by two merchants and a reviewer's listing of the 2018 as Palmela, while one British merchant lists the 2023 as Península de Setúbal, so the integrator may wish to confirm the latest label; no plain Dona Ermelinda red was found in the searches.

The grapes are the house's own blog and two merchants; one review gives Castelão, Touriga Nacional, Syrah and Cabernet for the 2013, hence the shift by vintage; the vines of fifty years and the making rest on two merchants' sheets that read alike and may share one source.

The founder is Deonilde in Portugal Global and the house's blog and Leonilde in others, and the order of the generations differs between accounts, so no early woman is named; the woman the house is named for is not named as a person, since her dates were not found, and her daughter and granddaughter are living.
The first bottled wine is Terras do Pó of 1997 in one magazine and around 2000 in another, so the story says the 1990s, which Forbes Portugal and Portugal Global both give for the turn to bottles.
The Grande Reserva's grapes and eighteen months are the house's own blog for the 2017; Castelão's share of the vineyard is left out as a present figure.
The region record's Fernando Pó and Castelão are borne out.

records.place: Quinta do Anjo, Palmela, Península de Setúbal

wine.name: Moscatel Roxo
wine.grapes: Moscatel Roxo, a pink skinned Muscat thought to be a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, at least the 85 per cent the name requires.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards around Quinta do Anjo, in the municipality of Palmela, on the Moscatel ground of the peninsula.
wine.making: The bunches are sorted with care and macerated for five days before fermentation, which runs slowly. Grape spirit stops it while the wine is sweet, and the wine then stays on its skins for about five months before it is finished in used French oak barrels of 225 litres, by its merchants' sheets.
wine.glass: Dark topaz; marmalade, caramel, vanilla and dried tobacco leaf, with a floral lift and sweet spices that grow with air; round, soft and fresh, with a very long finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its time in wood; the older, longer aged bottlings of the house, its Excellent among them, show what further years in cask give.
wine.serve: About 10 to 16 degrees Celsius, cooler as an aperitif and warmer after dinner; no decanting; a small white wine glass.

label.means: A traditional name allowed only when Moscatel Roxo gives at least 85 per cent of the must.
The designation of the peninsula's fortified Moscatels, delimited since 1907.

records.table: Casa Agrícola Horácio Simões, a family house of 1910 at Quinta do Anjo, says it backed Moscatel Roxo when the pink Muscat had all but vanished. Its Moscatel Roxo is fortified, left months on its skins and finished in old French oak: marmalade, caramel, a long finish.
records.story: The Setúbal peninsula was delimited for its Moscatel in 1907, and in 1910, by the house's own account, its founder began Casa Agrícola Horácio Simões at Quinta do Anjo, in the municipality of Palmela; three generations of the family have run it since. It makes the peninsula's range, Moscatel de Setúbal among its reds and whites, and its own pages speak of a policy of backing new products, one above all: Moscatel Roxo, a pink skinned Muscat that had all but disappeared from the region when the house chose to make it. Wines of Portugal describes the vine as thought to be a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, the small berried Muscat, and so a different vine from the Muscat of Alexandria behind ordinary Moscatel de Setúbal. The rules of the designation, set out again in 2009, allow the name Moscatel Roxo only when that grape gives at least 85 per cent of the must. The house's Moscatel Roxo is made in the Setúbal way, fortified and then left for months on its skins, and finished in used French oak barrels, and the house also keeps older bottlings of it. For a sommelier it is the pink Muscat in a family's hands: a rarer vine than the peninsula's own Moscatel, which this house, by its own account, chose to bring back.

others.name: Moscatel de Setúbal Superior 10 Anos
others.note: The house's ten year old Moscatel de Setúbal, a Superior aged in wood.

others.name: Moscatel Roxo Excellent
others.note: An older bottling of the house's Moscatel Roxo, aged longer in used French oak.

traps: Moscatel Roxo is a pink skinned Muscat thought to be a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, not a coloured form of Muscat of Alexandria.
Roxo names the pink skin of the grape: Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal is a sweet fortified wine, not a rosé.

cards.front: Horácio Simões Moscatel Roxo: what kind of vine is Moscatel Roxo?
cards.back: A pink skinned Muscat thought to be a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, the small berried Muscat.

cards.front: What does Casa Agrícola Horácio Simões say it did for Moscatel Roxo?
cards.back: It backed the grape and made its wine when the vine had all but disappeared from the region.

questions.q: A guest asks how much Moscatel Roxo a wine must hold for Horácio Simões to print Moscatel Roxo on its label. What is the rule?

At least 67 per cent of the must

Every grape in the must

In Vila Nogueira de Azeitão
In the port town of Setúbal
At Pegões, on the eastern plain

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 50, one on the house's own domain, besides the group's shared searches on the rules and the grape; one went to a writer's own site, which is not cited; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1910 and the founding are the house's own pages and two merchants; the revival is the house's own claim (a grape it found extinct in the region) with one merchant's note behind it, so it is told as the house's; the label is Moscatel Roxo under DO Setúbal, vintage dated in some bottlings (2008, 2013, 2014) and without a vintage in others.

The founder is José Carvalho Simões in most accounts and José Horácio Simões in one, and no dates were found, so he is described, not named; the two family winemakers listed by merchants are living and never named.

The making (five days' maceration before fermentation, about five months on the skins after fortification, used 225 litre French oak) rests on Vinha, Radar Wine and Wine House Portugal, merchants whose texts may share the house's sheet; no sheet of the house's own was found.
The 85 per cent rule is the IVV's page and Portaria 793/2009 of 28 July 2009; the minimum time in wood is 18 months in one account and 36 months for Roxo in another, so it is left out.

Codex in tension: the Setúbal region record's card calls Moscatel Roxo the rare pink skinned relative of Muscat of Alexandria; Wines of Portugal and the portaria's synonym Moscatel Galego Roxo place it with the small berried Muscat, a mutation of Moscatel Galego Branco, reported and not edited.
One merchant advises 18 degrees Celsius; the record follows José Maria da Fonseca's 10 to 16 for its Moscatel, for want of the house's own figure.
Medals are left out; the story's two dated turning points are 1907, 1910 and 2009.

records.place: Santo Isidro de Pegões, Montijo, Península de Setúbal

wine.name: Colheita Seleccionada Branco
wine.grapes: Fernão Pires, about a third, with Verdelho and Antão Vaz and smaller shares of Chardonnay and Arinto, by the co-operative's sheet.
wine.sites: The vineyards of the co-operative's growers on the sandy plain around Pegões, land the state divided among settler families of its agricultural colony and planted with vines.
wine.making: After a light maceration on the skins, the must ferments in French and American oak barrels, and the wine rests there on its fine lees for three to four months by vintage, the lees stirred regularly, before bottling.
wine.glass: Apricot, pineapple and pear with white blossom and a creamy, nutty touch of the barrel, lifted by fresh citrus acidity; supple and round, more texture than weight.
wine.ageing: Bottled young and made to drink young, while its fruit is fresh, within a few years of the harvest.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, as the co-operative's sheet advises; no decanting; a white wine glass.

label.means: Selected harvest: the name of the range, made red and white; spelt Selecionada on the co-operative's recent sheets.
The regional wine of the whole peninsula, with a wider list of grapes than its two DOCs.
The trading name of the Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões.

records.table: Adega de Pegões, the co-operative of the Pegões plain, makes its Colheita Seleccionada Branco from Fernão Pires with Verdelho, Antão Vaz, Chardonnay and Arinto, fermented in oak and rested there on its lees. Creamy and fresh, it suits fried fish and shellfish.
records.story: Adega de Pegões grew out of a settlement scheme. The state's Junta de Colonização Interna, created in 1936, chose the Herdade de Pegões, estates a brewing magnate had given to Lisbon's hospitals, and in the 1950s built an agricultural colony there: houses, land and vines for settler families from across the country, with its own church of Santo Isidro. The Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões received its charter on 7 March 1958 to serve those settlers, taking in their grapes and making their wine with the state's financial and technical help. After the revolution of 1974 it was taken over, and by its own account it went through years of upheaval in 1975 and 1976 before a long modernisation of its cellars, its fermentation vats and its bottling lines. Trading as Adega de Pegões, it makes red, white and fortified wines from its members' vineyards on the sandy plain, and its Colheita Seleccionada, made red and white, is a label its merchants abroad have listed vintage after vintage. The white blends Fernão Pires with Verdelho, Antão Vaz, Chardonnay and Arinto, fermented in oak and stirred on its lees. For a sommelier Pegões shows the peninsula's co-operative side: the grapes of many settler families, made in one cellar and sold under one name.

others.name: Colheita Seleccionada Tinto
others.note: The red of the range, a blend that changes by vintage, Syrah, Touriga Nacional and Cabernet Sauvignon in most years, aged in oak.

others.name: Adega de Pegões Moscatel de Setúbal
others.note: The co-operative's fortified Moscatel of the peninsula.

traps: Adega de Pegões is the trading name of a co-operative, the Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões, not a private estate.
The Colheita Seleccionada is made red and white: the white is led by Fernão Pires, the red a changing blend of Syrah, Touriga Nacional and Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.front: Adega de Pegões: what is the co-operative's full name, and when was it chartered?
cards.back: The Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões, chartered on 7 March 1958.

cards.front: Colheita Seleccionada Branco of Adega de Pegões: which grape leads the blend?
cards.back: Fernão Pires, with Verdelho, Antão Vaz, Chardonnay and Arinto.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Colheita Seleccionada Branco of Adega de Pegões feels creamy. Which step in its making explains it?
opts: Fermentation and a few months on fine lees in oak
Long ageing under a veil of flor yeast
A second fermentation in the bottle
Weeks of skin contact in clay jars
questions.exp: It ferments in French and American oak and rests three to four months on its fine lees, which are stirred, giving the creamy texture; it sees neither flor nor a second fermentation in bottle.

questions.q: Adega de Pegões received its charter in 1958 to serve a particular group of growers. Who were they?
opts: Settlers of a state agricultural colony
Tenants of a royal hunting estate
Monks of a nearby monastery
Growers bound to a Port shipper
questions.exp: The co-operative was set up to take in and make the grapes of the settlers of the colony the Junta de Colonização Interna built at Pegões in the 1950s; no monastery or royal estate was involved.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's share of 50, one on the co-operative's own domain, one restricted to a wrong domain that returned nothing; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: the white is taught, as the co-operative's own sheet and The Wine Society's listings of many vintages give it a steady blend and making, while the red's grapes change from vintage to vintage across the listings (Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Touriga Nacional, with Trincadeira, Aragonez or Alicante Bouschet in some years); the red goes in others; the full name is the Cooperativa Agrícola de Santo Isidro de Pegões and the charter is of 7 March 1958, by its own pages, with 1958 on The Wine Society's.

The label name: the plan and The Wine Society spell Seleccionada, the co-operative's recent sheets and some competition listings Selecionada, under the spelling reform; the record keeps the plan's spelling and says so on the label.

The time in wood is three months on the current sheet, four in an older one and in a merchant's sheet for the 2019, hence three to four by vintage; the serving temperature is the co-operative's sheet.

The brewing magnate is José Rovisco Pais by the co-operative and The Wine Society; his dates were not found, so he is described, not named; the Junta de Colonização Interna of 1936 and the colony of the 1950s are two academic theses of Évora, with the Montijo council's heritage route for the church and the co-operative; the colony's 207 families and its plan of 1942 rest on one source each and are left out.

The appellation of the white is Península de Setúbal on The Wine Society's listings and the co-operative's sheet; the red is listed as Palmela by one Canadian merchant against Península de Setúbal elsewhere, which matters only to the others line.
The winemaker named by merchants is living and never named; the co-operative's present size and turnover are left out.
